title: Hall Divisor and Hall Subgroup Definitions
content: Two central definitions formalize Hall's theory. IsHallDivisor d n captures the coprimeness condition: d divides n AND d is coprime to n/d, meaning the prime factors of n are partitioned into two disjoint sets — those dividing d and those not. IsHallSubgroup H formalizes that H is a Hall subgroup: its order and index are coprime, i.e., H contains exactly the p-Sylow components for a chosen subset of primes.
mathContext: A Hall divisor satisfies $\gcd(d, n/d) = 1$. Equivalently, for each prime $p$, either $p^{v_p(n)} \mid d$ or $\gcd(p, d) = 1$ — the full $p$-power goes entirely to $d$ or entirely to $n/d$. A Hall subgroup $H$ satisfies $\gcd(|H|, [G:H]) = 1$, generalizing Sylow subgroups from a single prime to a set of primes.

title: Primes Are Hall Divisors When Not Squared
content: A prime p is a Hall divisor of n exactly when p divides n but p² does not — when p appears with multiplicity exactly 1. The proof uses Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd to translate coprimality with n/p into the non-divisibility of p | (n/p), then lifts that to p² ∤ n via the divisibility chain.
mathContext: For a prime $p$: $\gcd(p, n/p) = 1 \iff p \nmid (n/p) \iff p^2 \nmid n$. This means Hall divisors at primes correspond precisely to squarefree prime factors. For $n = p^k m$ with $\gcd(p,m)=1$ and $k \geq 2$, the prime $p$ is NOT a Hall divisor of $n$ because $p^{k-1}$ shares the factor $p$ with $p$.

title: Trivial Hall Subgroups: The Boundary Cases
content: The trivial subgroup ⊥ = {1} is always a Hall subgroup (order 1, coprime to everything). G itself is always a Hall subgroup (index 1, coprime to everything). These boundary cases are proved by explicit card computations: Nat.card ⊥ = 1 uses Unique instance for the bottom subgroup; index ⊤ = 1 from Subgroup.index_top.
mathContext: $\gcd(1, n) = 1$ for all $n$ (trivial subgroup), and $\gcd(n, 1) = 1$ for all $n$ (full group with index 1). These correspond to $d=1$ and $d=|G|$, which are always Hall divisors: $\gcd(1, n) = 1$ and $\gcd(n, 1) = 1$.

title: Prime Case via Cauchy's Theorem
content: For prime p dividing |G|, the subgroup zpowers(x) generated by any element x of order p is the required subgroup of order p. This uses exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card (Cauchy's theorem in Mathlib) to produce x with orderOf x = p, then Nat.card_zpowers to convert the cyclic subgroup's card to its generator's order.
mathContext: Cauchy's theorem: if prime $p \mid |G|$, then $G$ has an element of order $p$. The subgroup $\langle x \rangle = \{1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^{p-1}\}$ has order $p$. This is a special case of Hall's theorem for $d = p$ a prime with $p^2 \nmid |G|$ not required — Cauchy is stronger in not requiring the Hall divisor condition.

title: Order of a Power: The Key Cyclic Calculation
content:
The private lemma orderOf_pow_div_of_dvd is the computational heart of the cyclic case. For an element g of order n, the power g^(n/d) has order exactly d. The proof chains orderOf_pow' (which gives orderOf(g^k) = n / gcd(n,k)) with Nat.gcd_eq_right (since d|n implies gcd(n, n/d) = d... wait, actually gcd(n, n/d) = n/d if d|n... let me re-read) — actually it rewrites gcd(orderOf g, orderOf g / d) = orderOf g / d using the fact that d | orderOf g, then uses Nat.div_div_self to simplify (n/d)/d... wait, let me re-read more carefully.

Actually: orderOf_pow' g k = orderOf(g) / gcd(orderOf g, k). With k = n/d, we get orderOf(g^(n/d)) = n / gcd(n, n/d). Since d|n, we have gcd(n, n/d) = n/d (the smaller divides the larger). So n / (n/d) = d. The proof uses Nat.gcd_eq_right (n/d | n) to simplify, then Nat.div_div_self.
mathContext: For $g$ with $\text{ord}(g) = n$ and $d \mid n$: $$\text{ord}(g^{n/d}) = \frac{n}{\gcd(n,\, n/d)} = \frac{n}{n/d} = d$$ since $\frac{n}{d} \mid n$ implies $\gcd(n, n/d) = n/d$. This is the fundamental computation connecting divisors of $|G|$ to cyclic subgroup orders.

title: Hall's Theorem for Cyclic Groups: Every Divisor Works
content: In cyclic groups, the Hall divisor condition is vacuous — every divisor d of |G| is a Hall divisor (since ℤ/nℤ has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n). The proof obtains the cyclic generator g from IsCyclic.exists_generator, verifies orderOf g = |G| using orderOf_eq_card_of_forall_mem_zpowers, then produces the subgroup zpowers(g^(|G|/d)) and applies the order calculation from the private lemma.
mathContext: For $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, every divisor $d \mid n$ is automatically a Hall divisor (since $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is squarefree-in-the-right-way isn't required — all divisors work in cyclic groups). The unique subgroup of order $d$ is $\langle g^{n/d} \rangle$ where $g$ is any generator. This is much stronger than Hall's theorem requires.

title: The Main Theorem: Axiomatized Pending Schur–Zassenhaus
content: Hall's theorem for solvable groups is stated as an axiom because its proof requires the Schur–Zassenhaus theorem — that if N is a normal Hall subgroup of G (i.e., gcd(|N|, [G:N]) = 1), then N has a complement — which is not in Mathlib 4.26. The proof outline in the docstring is mathematically complete: induct on |G|, use minimal normal subgroup N ≅ (ℤ/pℤ)^k, and handle the two cases p|d and p∤d via Schur–Zassenhaus lifting.
mathContext: The Schur–Zassenhaus theorem states: if $N \unlhd G$ with $\gcd(|N|, [G:N]) = 1$, then $G = N \rtimes H$ for some subgroup $H$ with $|H| = [G:N]$ (a complement to $N$). Hall's inductive proof uses this to lift Hall subgroups from $G/N$ back to $G$. The axiom `hall_solvable` encodes the complete theorem with 2 axioms total (including `hall_characterizes_solvability`).

title: Sharpness: A₅ Has No Subgroup of Order 15
content: The alternating group A₅ on 5 elements has order 60 = 4·3·5. The number 15 = 3·5 is a Hall divisor of 60 (gcd(15, 4) = 1), but A₅ has no subgroup of order 15. This is because A₅ is the smallest non-abelian simple group, hence not solvable, and it demonstrates that Hall's theorem fails for non-solvable groups. The proof uses alternatingGroup.not_solvable which is directly available in Mathlib.
mathContext: $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$. Hall divisors include $15 = 3 \cdot 5$ with $\gcd(15, 4) = 1$. But $A_5$ has no subgroup of order 15: such a subgroup would be normal (index 4, and $A_5$ acts on cosets giving a homomorphism $A_5 \to S_4$, forcing the kernel to be normal of order 15, contradicting simplicity). This proves solvability is necessary.

title: Hall's Converse: Solvability Characterized by Subgroup Existence
content: The second axiom axiomatizes the striking converse: G is solvable if and only if Hall subgroups exist for every Hall divisor. The forward direction is hall_solvable above; the converse is deep and uses the Feit–Thompson odd-order theorem (every group of odd order is solvable) as a key ingredient. This characterization makes Hall's theorem not just a generalization of Sylow theory but a complete characterization of solvability.
mathContext: The biconditional $G$ solvable $\iff$ Hall subgroups exist for all Hall divisors captures a profound structural insight. The converse proof proceeds: if Hall subgroups exist for all Hall divisors, check every prime order subgroup (Hall divisors for squarefree primes), use their existence to build a composition series with abelian factors. Crucially it uses that groups of odd order are solvable (Feit–Thompson, 1963).

title: Concrete Hall Divisor Calculations
content: Three worked examples ground the abstract theory: (1) 30 = 2·3·5 is squarefree, so ALL its divisors are Hall divisors — every divisor d has gcd(d, 30/d) = 1 since no prime appears twice. (2) 12 = 4·3: divisors 2 and 6 are NOT Hall divisors because gcd(2, 6) = 2 ≠ 1. (3) 60 = 4·3·5: Hall divisors include 15 = 3·5 (gcd = 1 with 4) but A₅ witnesses the failure for non-solvable groups. All proofs go through by norm_num.
mathContext: For $n = 30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$: $\gcd(6, 5)=1$, $\gcd(10, 3)=1$, $\gcd(15, 2)=1$ — squarefree $\Rightarrow$ all divisors are Hall divisors. For $n = 12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$: $\gcd(2, 6) = 2 \neq 1$ (since $2 \mid 6$), $\gcd(6, 2) = 2 \neq 1$ — non-squarefree part causes Hall divisors to be restricted to $\{1, 3, 4, 12\}$.
